The Daggertooth pike conger Muraenesox cinereus is a large, predatory anguilliform fish that supports significant fisheries across the Indo-Pacific region. Field surveys indicate that this species attains a maximum recorded body length of 220 centimeters [Li = 220 centimeters], making it one of the largest members of the family Muraenesocidae. The size structure of exploited populations reveals that puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation, is reached at a total length of 93.2 centimeters [Lp = 93.2 centimeters], a threshold that appears to be reached after several years of somatic growth in continental shelf habitats. Individuals of this species are iteroparous and exhibit a relatively protracted reproductive lifespan, a pattern consistent with other large-bodied, slow-growing teleosts inhabiting subtropical and tropical waters. The length-weight relationship derived from captured specimens indicates that a fish attaining the ultimate length would weigh approximately 67.9 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 67.9 kilograms], reflecting the substantial energetic investment required to reach such dimensions in a piscivorous, bentho-pelagic predator. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the typical age at first reproduction likely occurs well after the attainment of the pubertal length threshold, and the species is thought to exhibit a relatively late age at maturity.

At the thermal conditions typical of its subtropical spawning grounds (17.4 °C [T = 17.4 °C]), the embryonic development of Muraenesox cinereus proceeds at a measured pace. Based on comparisons with the congener Congresox talabonoides, for which egg diameters range from 1.7 to 2.2 millimeters, the estimated wet weight of a newly hatched yolk-sac larva of the Daggertooth pike conger is approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams], a value typical of pelagic marine teleost eggs that undergo lecithotrophic development. The incubation period at this stable temperature regime has been documented to last approximately 19 days [ab = approximately 19 days] from the moment of gamete fusion to the eclosion o at a temperature of 17.4 °C [T = 17.4 °C]f the prolarva. This duration is consistent with the temperature-dependent developmental rates observed in other anguilliform species that spawn in the upper water column of continental slope waters. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, or alevin, relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the initial phase following chorion rupture, with the progressive yolk utilization supporting organogenesis and the development of the functional mouth gape that marks the onset of exogenous feeding.

Reproductive output in the Daggertooth pike conger has been characterized through histological examination of gravid females captured during the spawning season. Under the prevailing water temperature of 17.4 °C [T = 17.4 °C], individual females produce between 3 and 5 egg batches per year [Ri = between 3 and 5 egg batches per year], with each spawning event yielding an estimated 200,000 to 300,000 hydrated oocytes [N_R_i = each spawning event yielding an estimated 200,000 to 300,000 hydrated oocytes] depending on female body size and condition. The maximum daily reproduction rate, calculated from the annual reproductive output, is approximately 10.5 oocytes per day [Ri = approximately 10.5 oocytes per day]. These values place the species among the more fecund members of the Muraenesocidae, with the high ovum production reflecting an adaptive response to high rates of larval mortality in the planktonic environment. The annual reproductive cycle appears to be synchronized with seasonal productivity patterns, ensuring that the timing of broadcast spawning events coincides with peak availability of suitable prey for the exogenously feeding larvae during the early pelagic larval phase. Such a strategy is common among large-bodied marine teleosts that produce numerous, small pelagic eggs.

The body mass trajectory of Muraenesox cinereus from puberty to its asymptotic size reveals a considerable scope for post-maturational growth. At the length of 93.2 centimeters corresponding to the pubertal threshold, the predicted wet body weight is approximately 4.9 kilograms [Wwp = approximately 4.9 kilograms], based on the species-specific length-weight conversion. In contrast, an individual that has achieved the ultimate total length of 220 centimeters would have a body mass of 67.9 kilograms [Wwi = 67.9 kilograms], an increase of nearly fourteen-fold relative to the mass at the onset of gonadal recrudescence. This pattern of pronounced indeterminate growth is characteristic of many large marine piscivores, allowing them to exploit increasingly larger prey items as they age and to achieve higher fecundity through increased body volume. The wet weight of a newly hatched larva, at approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams], is minuscule relative to the adult mass, representing a growth increment of over seven orders of magnitude during the species' ontogeny. This immense size increase is supported by a diet that shifts from copepods and other zooplankton in the larval period to fish and cephalopods in the juvenile and adult stages.

Longevity estimates for the Daggertooth pike conger, derived from mark-recapture studies and analysis of opercular bone annuli, indicate that the maximum lifespan at the species' typical environmental temperature of 17.4 °C [T = 17.4 °C] is approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years]. This lifespan is consistent with that of other large, slow-growing anguilliform predators that inhabit continental shelf and slope environments. The post-reproductive phase in this species is relatively brief, with senescent individuals showing signs of physiological deterioration, including reduced feeding activity and increased susceptibility to parasitic infections. The combination of a size at puberty of 93.2 centimeters [Lp = 93.2 centimeters] total length and a maximum total length of 220 centimeters [Li = 220 centimeters] suggests that individuals continue to grow throughout most of their adult lives, allocating substantial resources to somatic growth even after the initiation of reproductive activity. This life-history strategy, characterized by delayed maturity, high fecundity, and a protracted growth phase, is typical of marine teleosts that experience low natural mortality rates once they reach the larger size classes, where predator gape limitation provides a refuge from most piscivorous threats.
